text.6: Geographic lysis • Focal • Well-defined (benign) or indistinct (more aggressive) margins • With or without cortical expansion • Shorter zone of transition between normal and abnormal, but not always well-defined • More apt to include benign differentials, e.g. bone cyst
text.8: Expansile lysis • A geographic region of lysis that expands beyond normal cortical margin shape • Soft tissue swelling centered at joint (intracapsular) • Periosteal proliferation at lytic margins indicating some evidence for “slow” growth • Smooth solid, well-defined periosteal proliferation - Codm
text.9: Moth-eaten lysis • Multiple regions of lysis varying in size and shape • Indistinct margins • Long zone of transition between normal and abnormal bone • More aggressive differential diagnoses (e.g. neoplasia, infection)
text.10: Permeative lysis • Very indistinct, pinpoint areas of lysis • Long zone of transition between normal and abnormal bone • Malignant neoplasia and uncontrolled osteomyelitis/infection
text.14: Solid • Can be smooth or irregular • Bone fills the space deep to periosteum • Well-defined or indistinct • Based on maturity, activity, and aggressiveness • Differentials are more benign • Continuous, low-grade trauma • Remodeling • Final stage of bone healing or other periosteal pattern
text.16: Lamellar • Repeated episodes of periosteal trauma • Sheets of new bone parallel to the cortex • Layered or “onion skin” appearance • Semi-aggressive • Seen in hypertrophic osteodystrophy (HOD)
text.17: Palisading or Columnar • Periosteal reaction at 90° angle to axis of bone • Often solid with variable margination • Malignant or benign differential diagnoses • Seen with hypertrophic osteopathy (periosteal reaction secondary to thoracic disease) or osteomyelitis (bacterial)
text.18: Spiculated or Sunburst • Thin spicules of new bone radiate from lesion • Periosteum/osteoblasts along Sharpey’s fibers are responsible for the appearance of the pattern • Aggressive lesion • Malignant neoplasia or infection
text.19: Amorphous • Random, indistinct, very disorganized periosteal bone formation • Aggressive and typically associated with malignancy
text.24: How can I tell if it’s a tumor or infection? • Short answer – you can’t • Cytology or histopathology
text.30: Soft tissue neoplasia/tumor invading bone • Joint/periarticular neoplasms • Synovial cell sarcoma • Histiocytic sarcoma • Lesion is centered at a joint • All adjacent bones can be affected
text.65: Fracture margins – chronicity • Affects repair plan/difficulty • Knowledge of bone modeling/remodeling • Fracture margin resorption causes rounded fracture margins (7 – 10 days) • New bone formation (10 – 14 days)

text.10: Nasal Rhinitis • Destructive rhinitis • Neoplasia • Fungal • Non-destructive rhinitis • Viral and bacterial, lymphocytic • Foreign bodies
text.14: Nasal aspergillosis • Destructive rhinitis • Younger (less than 4 years of age) • Non-brachycephalic dogs • Lysis of conchae with punctate lucencies of bone • Increased localized soft-tissue opacity of the nasal • Frontal sinus involvement variable
text.23: Spondylosis deformans • Non-inflammatory degeneration of peripheral endplate region • Mineralization of ventral longitudinal ligament and entheses • Unclear clinical significance
